item.title: Bill Cassidy Will Back Todd Blanche as Attorney General, Salvaging His Confirmation
item.description: The Louisiana senator said that, despite reservations, he would back President Trump’s pick for attorney general, giving Republicans enough votes for a majority.
item.dc:creator: Michael Gold and Carl Hulse
item.media:credit: Alex Kent/The New York Times
item.media:description: Senator Bill Cassidy, Republican of Louisiana, said on Friday that he had come to believe that Todd Blanche would be better positioned to push back against President Trump’s demands than an alternative.

item.title: Prosecutor Sues Justice Dept. Over Dismissal After Right-Wing Influencer’s Claim
item.description: Will Rosenzweig joins a growing list of former prosecutors and federal agents who have gone to court to contest the purge of law enforcement deemed disloyal.
item.dc:creator: Alan Feuer
item.media:credit: Alex Kent/The New York Times
item.media:description: The Justice Department in September fired Will Rosenzweig, a prosecutor who had earned consistent praise, hours after a right-wing commentator demanded on social media that officials dismiss him.

item.title: Don Lemon Accuses Justice Dept. of Vindictive Prosecution in Church Protest Case
item.description: Lawyers for the former CNN anchor asked a judge to throw out the case, saying prosecutors had “acted on the president’s animus by filing unprecedented charges against a journalist for doing his job.”
item.dc:creator: Alan Feuer
item.media:credit: Tom Baker/Associated Press
item.media:description: Don Lemon, center, outside court in St. Paul, Minn., in February. “The record could not be more clear that Mr. Lemon has been a persistent target of President Trump’s ire before the events in Minnesota,” his lawyers wrote.

item.title: Weak Jobs Report Does Not Eliminate Prospects of Interest Rate Rise
item.description: Officials at the Federal Reserve are chiefly focused on the trajectory of inflation after five years of overshooting the central bank’s 2 percent target.
item.dc:creator: Colby Smith
item.media:credit: Anna Rose Layden for The New York Times
item.media:description: Kevin M. Warsh, the Federal Reserve chairman, has pledged to make delivering price stability the primary focus of his tenure.

item.title: The Bond Market Is Signaling Rising Risks. Investors Should Listen.
item.description: While the Fed didn’t raise rates, the bond market did. That means hardship for home buyers and higher hurdles for A.I. data centers and the stock market. But it’s also a boon for retirees.

item.title: Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan Sign Joint Defense Pact

item.title: Voter-Registration Error Could Cost Immigrants a Shot at a Green Card
item.description: New Jersey improperly added as many as 6,600 noncitizens to its voter rolls. Those people could now be forced out of the country.
item.dc:creator: Tracey Tully
item.media:credit: Karsten Moran for The New York Times
item.media:description: New Jersey continues to deal with the fallout of thousands of noncitizens — as many as 6,600, according to the governor — having been added to its voter rolls.

item.title: Luigi Mangione Is Facing Two Trials. Isn’t That Double Jeopardy?
item.description: The legal principle prevents a person from being tried twice for the same crime. But Mr. Mangione’s situation shows how complicated the judicial system can be.
item.dc:creator: Hurubie Meko
item.media:credit: Jeenah Moon/Reuters
item.media:description: Luigi Mangione is facing both a state and federal trial in relation to the killing of Brian Thompson, but the U.S. Constitution says that a defendant can’t be tried or the same crime twice. However, there are some exceptions.
